chapters.title: Chapter 3: Valuing a Company With No Market Price

lessons.title: Cap Tables, Funding Rounds and Dilution Explained

children.text: A departing early employee at Vayu Mobility, the same company once pitched to Meena over WhatsApp as a "pre-IPO" opportunity, now genuinely wants to sell her some of his vested, exercised shares. This time Meena has done real diligence: SPA, RoFR clearance, the works. Her venture-capitalist friend asks one more question before she wires anything. "Do you actually know what percentage of the company you're buying, and what class of share it is?" Meena realises she has been quoted a price, but never actually seen the cap table behind it.

body.text: A percentage ownership number is meaningless on its own. What matters is the share class behind it, and what round comes after yours, because both can dilute or subordinate your stake without you selling a single share.

children.text: What a Cap Table Actually Is

markDefs.definition: The complete ledger of who owns a company's shares, in what class, across every funding round.
A share count or ownership percentage that includes not just shares currently issued, but also shares reserved for the ESOP pool that have not yet been exercised.

children.text: A
cap table

is simply the full ledger of who owns a company: every shareholder, the class of share they hold, how many shares, and what percentage of the company that represents. Percentages are almost always quoted on a
fully diluted

basis, meaning the calculation includes not just shares actually issued, but also shares reserved for the ESOP pool that employees have not yet exercised. This matters because it is the standard basis everyone in the room, founders, investors, and any buyer, is expected to use when talking about ownership.

body.caption: Vayu Mobility's cap table before its Series E round (illustrative)

children.text: Notice the ESOP Pool line: those 15,00,000 shares are the options reserved for employees, including ones not yet exercised. If Meena buys shares from a departing employee, she is buying shares that have already moved out of that pooled line and into the employee's own name, but the pool itself, and its effect on everyone's percentage, does not disappear just because one employee's options were exercised.
How a Funding Round Actually Changes the Cap Table

Every new funding round follows the same basic mechanics. The company and new investors agree on a pre-money valuation, the value assigned to the company before the new money arrives. The investment amount is added to get the post-money valuation. Dividing the pre-money valuation by the number of fully diluted shares that existed before the round gives the price per share, and dividing the investment amount by that price per share gives the number of brand new shares the round creates.

body.latex: \text{Price per Share} = \dfrac{\text{Pre-money Valuation}}{\text{Pre-round Fully Diluted Shares}}
body.caption: Step 2: Price per share is set from the pre-money valuation, before the new money arrives
Step 3: How many new shares the round actually creates

children.text: Worked Example: Vayu Mobility's Series E

Suppose Vayu Mobility raises a fresh Series E round at a pre-money valuation of ₹6,000 crore, with new investors putting in ₹960 crore. Post-money valuation is ₹6,960 crore. Price per share is ₹6,000 crore divided by the pre-round 1,25,00,000 fully diluted shares, which works out to ₹4,800 per share. At that price, ₹960 crore buys the new investors exactly 20,00,000 new shares, taking the total fully diluted share count to 1,45,00,000.

body.caption: Before and after the Series E round

body.text: Look closely at the founders' and ESOP pool's rows. Neither sold a single share, and their share counts did not change at all. Their percentage ownership still fell, from 32% to 27.6% for founders and from 12% to 10.3% for the ESOP pool, purely because the total number of shares in existence grew. This is dilution: it happens automatically whenever new shares are issued, whether or not you personally sold anything.

body.title: Check Your Understanding: Series E Ownership
body.prompt: Vayu Mobility's Series E issues 20,00,000 new shares, taking the post-round fully diluted total to 1,45,00,000 shares. What percentage of the company do the Series E investors own immediately after the round? Answer to one decimal place.
body.explanation: 20,00,000 ÷ 1,45,00,000 = 0.1379, or 13.8%. This is simply the new investors' share count divided by the new, larger total, the same fully diluted logic applied to every other row in the cap table.

children.text: The Part Most Secondary Buyers Miss: What Class of Share Are You Actually Buying?

markDefs.definition: Compulsorily Convertible Preference Shares, the instrument most institutional investors receive, which convert to common equity but carry a liquidation preference until conversion or exit.
A contractual right letting certain shareholders, typically CCPS holders, be paid a set amount before common shareholders receive anything in an exit or liquidation.

children.text: The cap table tells you a percentage. It does not tell you what happens to that percentage in a weak outcome, and that depends on share class, not ownership percentage. Founders and ESOP holders in the table above hold plain common equity. Every institutional round from Seed through Series E holds
CCPS
, Compulsorily Convertible Preference Shares, which almost always carry a
liquidation preference

, a contractual right to be paid a set amount, commonly at least their original investment, before common shareholders receive anything in an exit or liquidation. When Meena buys shares from a departing employee, she is buying common equity, the exact class that ranks behind every one of those preference rounds.

body.caption: Who gets paid first in an exit: a simplified waterfall

cells: Series D and E CCPS holders (most recent rounds)
Their liquidation preference, typically at least their original investment, ahead of everyone else
Seed through Series C CCPS holders
Their own liquidation preference, in an order set by the shareholders' agreement
Common shareholders (founders, ESOP/employee shares, and any secondary buyer of those shares)
Whatever proceeds remain, split pro-rata by ownership percentage

body.text: If you buy common equity shares from an employee at a price implied by the company's last funding round valuation, you are, in effect, paying a preference-round price for a share that sits behind every preference round in a downside scenario. In a strong exit this difference may not matter much. In a weak one, it can be the entire difference between getting your money back and getting nothing.

body.title: A Weak Exit, Worked Through
body.scenario: Vayu Mobility is eventually acquired for ₹5,000 crore, well below its last private round's implied valuation. Across all its funding rounds, CCPS investors are collectively owed ₹4,800 crore in liquidation preference, ahead of everyone else.
body.prompt: What happens to the founders, ESOP holders, and any secondary buyer of common shares in this scenario, and why does it matter that Meena specifically bought common shares, not CCPS?
body.modelAnswer: Only ₹200 crore (₹5,000 crore minus the ₹4,800 crore preference claim) is left for every common shareholder combined: founders, ESOP holders, and anyone who bought common shares from them secondhand, however large their combined percentage ownership looks on the cap table. A common shareholder's percentage stake only matters after the preference stack is fully cleared. Because Meena specifically bought common shares, the class an employee could actually sell her, rather than CCPS, she is directly exposed to exactly this scenario, even though the price she paid was benchmarked to a valuation that assumed a far better outcome for everyone.

body.title: Where Common Shares Rank
body.question: A secondary buyer purchases common equity shares from a startup's early employee. In a weak exit where sale proceeds fall short of the total CCPS liquidation preference owed to institutional investors, what happens to the buyer's shares?
options: They are paid out first, since common shareholders founded the company
They receive nothing, or close to nothing, since CCPS holders' liquidation preference is paid before common shareholders receive anything
They are automatically converted to CCPS and receive the same treatment as institutional investors
The exit price is legally required to be split strictly by cap table percentage, regardless of share class
body.explanation: Liquidation preference is paid to CCPS holders before any proceeds reach common shareholders. If the exit price does not even cover the full preference stack, common shareholders, including any secondary buyer of common shares, can receive little or nothing, regardless of their percentage ownership on the cap table.

body.title: Naming the Right
body.textWithBlank: A share class that must be paid a fixed amount before common shareholders receive anything in an exit or liquidation is said to carry a ___.
body.explanation: Liquidation preference is what lets CCPS and other preference holders jump ahead of common shareholders in the payout order.

children.text: Questions to Ask Before Trusting a Cap-Table-Based Price

body.title: Before You Trust a Price Benchmarked to the Cap Table
steps: Ask exactly which share class you are buying: common/equity or a form of preference share (CCPS)
Ask whether the seller's shares carry any liquidation preference, or rank behind those that do
Ask how large the total CCPS liquidation preference stack is relative to the company's last valuation
Remember that a percentage ownership figure means little until you know where your share class ranks in an exit
Do not assume a "discount to last valuation" is a bargain if you are buying a share class that is more exposed than the valuation implies

children.text: Putting the Cap Table to Work

Reading a cap table properly means three things: checking ownership on a fully diluted basis, tracking how each new round dilutes everyone who came before, and understanding exactly where your own share class ranks if the eventual outcome is a weak one. A percentage on its own answers none of that.

body.title: Cap Tables and Dilution: Key Terms

cards.definition: The complete ledger of who owns a company's shares, in what class, across every funding round.
The total share count including all outstanding shares plus reserved but unexercised ESOP pool shares, used as the denominator for ownership percentages.
The reduction in an existing shareholder's ownership percentage caused by a company issuing new shares, even though the shareholder's own share count is unchanged.
Pre-money is a company's agreed valuation before a new investment; post-money is pre-money plus the new investment amount.
Compulsorily Convertible Preference Shares, the instrument most institutional investors receive, which convert to common equity but carry a liquidation preference until conversion or exit.
A contractual right letting certain shareholders, typically CCPS holders, be paid a set amount before common shareholders receive anything in an exit or liquidation.

points: A cap table is the full ledger of who owns what class of share, across every funding round. Ownership percentage alone, without knowing the share class, tells you very little.
Every new funding round dilutes existing shareholders' percentage ownership, even though their actual share count never changes.
Post-money valuation equals pre-money valuation plus the new investment; price per share is set from the pre-money valuation and the pre-round fully diluted share count.

Institutional investors typically hold CCPS with a liquidation preference, paid out before common shareholders in an exit. Founders, employees, and most secondary buyers of ESOP or founder shares typically hold plain common equity, which ranks behind that preference stack.

A price benchmarked to the company's last funding round valuation does not account for where your specific share class ranks in a weak exit. Always ask what class of share you are actually buying before treating a valuation-based price as fair.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Vayu Mobility, its cap table, and all figures shown are fictional and illustrative, constructed to demonstrate the mechanics of dilution and liquidation preference, not real market data. Real cap tables, funding terms, and waterfall structures vary company to company and should be reviewed with a qualified professional before any real transaction.
